summary: The third part of Privacy Enhanced Mail. It gives definitions, references, and identifiers for the algorithms and usage modes used by RFC 1113 and RFC 1114. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1423.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the list of locking methods the secret-mail rules are allowed to use, with a name for each.

subtitle: Algorithm identifiers and specifications for Privacy Enhanced Mail.

tldr.problem: Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) needs to specify which encryption and authentication algorithms implementors may use, along with their identifiers for mail headers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1115 catalogs the symmetric algorithms (DES in various modes), asymmetric algorithms (RSA), and integrity check algorithms (MAC and RSA-MD2) permitted in PEM, assigning each a string identifier.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1115 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 1423 as part of the PEM suite upgrade. Modern email encryption uses S/MIME.

today: RFC 1115 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 1423, which updated the algorithm selections for PEM. Later, S/MIME became the standard for email encryption and authentication, superseding PEM entirely. However, MD2 and RSA remain important in other cryptographic applications.

sections.title: Algorithm Catalog for Privacy Enhanced Mail
sections.content:
Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) is a framework for secure electronic mail developed by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) Privacy Task Force. The core PEM specifications are RFC 1113 (general concepts), RFC 1114 (procedures), and RFC 1115 (algorithms and identifiers). RFC 1115 provides the technical details about which encryption and authentication algorithms PEM implementations may use.

This RFC serves as a reference for implementors and defines the character string identifiers that appear in PEM message headers to declare which algorithms were used. By centralizing algorithm specifications in a separate document, the PEM standards can be updated for algorithms independently of the main protocol rules. The document covers symmetric encryption (DES), asymmetric encryption (RSA), and integrity check algorithms (MAC and RSA-MD2).
sections.plainLanguage: PEM is a way to send secret email. This document lists all the different encryption methods you can use and gives each one an official name.

sections.title: Symmetric Encryption: DES Modes
sections.content:
All symmetric encryption algorithms defined in RFC 1115 are different usage modes of the Data Encryption Standard (DES), also called DEA-1. DES is a single-key block cipher with a 64-bit block size. The RFC specifies three modes of operation.

DES-ECB (Electronic Codebook mode) encrypts each 64-bit block independently using the same key. It is simple but less secure because identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks. DES-ECB is used only for encrypting the Data Encryption Key (DEK) and Message Integrity Check (MIC) values, never for message text.

DES-EDE (Encrypt-Decrypt-Encrypt mode), as defined in ANSI X9.17, applies DES encryption, then decryption, then encryption again using a pair of 64-bit keys. This triple operation strengthens the encryption and is also used only for DEK and MIC encryption.

DES-CBC (Cipher Block Chaining mode) links each ciphertext block to the next using an initialization vector, so identical plaintext blocks produce different ciphertext. CBC mode is used exclusively for encrypting message text because it provides better security than ECB.
sections.plainLanguage: DES is the main encryption method. ECB is simplest but weak. CBC is better for messages. EDE is stronger for protecting the encryption keys themselves.

sections.title: Asymmetric Encryption: RSA
sections.content:
RFC 1115 specifies RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) as the only asymmetric (public-key) encryption algorithm for PEM. RSA uses a public key (the product of two large primes) and a private key to encrypt and decrypt data. In PEM, RSA is used to encrypt the DEK (Data Encryption Key) and the MIC (Message Integrity Check), allowing a sender to send the same encrypted message to multiple recipients by encrypting the symmetric key once for each recipient's public key.

The RFC specifies that a recipient's public key includes a modulus and a public exponent (either 3 or 65537). When encrypting, if the data is shorter than the modulus, it is padded with zeros on the left. For multi-recipient messages using the exponent 3, the RFC recommends a different approach: a separate pseudorandom padding value should be generated for each recipient to prevent certain attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: RSA is a two-key system: one key is public (everyone knows it), one is private (only you know it). PEM uses it to send the same secret message to many people by encrypting the key once for each person.

sections.title: Integrity Check Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 1115 defines two algorithms for computing Message Integrity Checks (MICs), which authenticate that a message has not been altered. The Message Authentication Code (MAC) uses DES in a special mode (defined in FIPS PUB 113) to generate a 64-bit integrity value. The MAC is computed using a variant of the DEK created by XORing the DEK with the hexadecimal constant F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0.

However, RFC 1115 strongly discourages using MAC for multi-recipient messages because it does not provide individual sender authentication; all authorized recipients could modify the message while preserving a valid MAC. For multi-recipient messages and for certificate integrity checks, RFC 1115 specifies RSA-MD2, a cryptographic hash algorithm that produces a 16-byte digest. MD2 was provided by Ron Rivest of RSA Data Security free of licensing restrictions specifically for use in PEM.
sections.plainLanguage: MAC is like a quick checksum that proves a message was not changed. MD2 is stronger and lets you prove who specifically sent the message. For messages to many people, MD2 is required.

sections.title: RSA-MD2 Message Digest
sections.content:
RFC 1115 includes a complete reference implementation of the RSA-MD2 message digest algorithm in C. MD2 accepts a message of any length and outputs a 16-byte (128-bit) digest. The algorithm works by processing the message in 16-byte chunks, maintaining internal buffers and a checksum register.

The algorithm uses a large substitution table (called S-table), derived from the digits of pi, to add nonlinearity to the computation. The implementation provided in the RFC serves as the authoritative definition; implementors may optimize it for their environment but must produce identical results. MD2 later became widely used in other cryptographic contexts before being superseded by more modern hash functions like SHA-1 and SHA-2.
sections.plainLanguage: MD2 is a recipe for turning any message into a short fingerprint that is very hard to forge. This fingerprint proves the message came from someone who knew the right secret key.
